text: An American monetary symbol, carried into its next form.
A century-long migration. Reasonably on schedule.
Buffalo are resilient. Incorrect transactions are not.
Long before it was money, the bison was a force of nature. Immense. Unbowed. Built to outlast whatever the plains could send against it.
A nation put it on its money to borrow that character, and each era carried it in the material of its time.
The fourth issue is minted on-chain: the same symbol, in the medium of this century.
The history is still being written.
Some memecoins begin with invented lore. BUFFALO arrived with archives.
For more than a century, the bison has marked American money. Here are three of its landmarks, and the fourth form. Each changed the material. None changed the animal.
The ten-dollar United States Note of 1901 places a bison at the center of the design, flanked by portraits of Meriwether Lewis and William Clark. Collectors still call it the Bison Note.
1901 United States Note, $10. Public-domain reproduction via Wikimedia Commons.
The symbol goes into every pocket.
James Earle Fraser’s Buffalo nickel takes the bison from a ten-dollar note to a five-cent coin, in everyday circulation from 1913 to 1938.
Portable conviction. Five cents at a time.
Buffalo nickel, reverse. Design by James Earle Fraser. Image: United States Mint.
The symbol returns in pure gold.
The United States Mint revives Fraser's design for the American Buffalo, the first .9999 fine, 24-karat gold coin the Mint ever struck.
American Buffalo gold coin, introduced 2006. Image: United States Mint.
$BUFFALO carries the same symbol into its fourth medium: a token minted on Solana. The material changes again. The animal does not.

Nations choose symbols for the qualities they want to be seen to have. The United States chose the bison for these.
The largest land mammal in North America. A bull can weigh up to a ton and still run at thirty-five miles an hour.
Tens of millions once crossed the plains. By 1900, fewer than a thousand remained. It came back.
Nothing about it asks permission. Not its size, not its stride, not its stare.
The nation did not invent these qualities. It borrowed them. The Fourth Issue returns them to the symbol.
Not a dog. Not a frog.
For a century, its power had borders. On the chain, it has none.
A banknote stops at a border. A coin is legal tender in one country. The Fourth Issue moves at the speed of a block, to anyone holding a wallet, anywhere on the map.
MAP DRAWN WITHOUT A SINGLE BORDER LINE.
Every era, struck into one coin.
The emblem carries the full provenance, past, present and what comes next, so that its era cannot be pinned down.
Bronze, for the metal issues: the nickel and the gold.
Greenback green, for the paper issue and the century of notes that followed.
Drawn in the intaglio tradition of banknote engraving. Not a mascot. A specimen.
The security pattern of paper money, redrawn as flowing, computed line. Engraving, as the future would draw it.
